claims.text: A targeted thermomechanical treatment can increase dislocation density in a refractory high-entropy alloy relative to standard annealing.
A targeted thermomechanical treatment can refine grain-boundary architecture and alter grain-boundary cohesion in a refractory high-entropy alloy.
The treatment-induced microstructure will significantly modify high-temperature thermoelastic behavior relative to an annealed baseline.
The treatment-induced microstructure will significantly modify high-temperature mechanical behavior relative to an annealed baseline.
A standard-annealed refractory HEA has moderate dislocation density and otherwise unmodified grain-boundary characteristics.
The comparison can hold alloy composition constant while changing dislocation density and grain-boundary cohesion through thermal or thermomechanical processing.
Increased dislocation density promotes dislocation pinning during high-temperature deformation.
Refined or cohesion-modified grain boundaries change grain-boundary slip activity during high-temperature deformation.
Dislocation morphology and density govern high-temperature mechanical properties in refractory HEAs.
The induced dislocation and grain-boundary changes alter yield strength and ductility during high-temperature deformation.
Treated samples will have greater high-temperature yield strength than standard-annealed samples.
Treated samples will exhibit a shift in ductility, potentially a reduction, relative to standard-annealed samples.
Treatment-related changes in dislocation density and diffraction patterns will accompany the mechanical-property changes.
The proposed mechanism applies at temperatures above 0.5 Tm under constant-strain-rate deformation.
Oxidation must be minimized to isolate intrinsic high-temperature deformation behavior.
Failure to observe a statistically significant dislocation-density increase accompanied by correlated yield-strength and ductility changes would falsify the hypothesis.
